result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers explain why the low change rate does not prove accuracy: the pre-selected category, Enter-to-approve, bulk approve and the throughput target all push reviewers toward agreeing. A is tighter and says outright that there is no reason shown for the suggestion. B covers more ground, adding time-on-row data, category-level skew hidden in the average, and a deliberate second action plus hiding the suggestion for risky rows. Neither proposes highlighting the passage that drove the category. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers make the same core argument: the pre-selected category, Enter-to-approve, bulk approve and throughput target turn the low change rate into a measure of agreement, not accuracy. Both also propose seeded known-wrong rows and blind sampling. B wins narrowly: it explicitly flags that no reason is shown for the suggestion, ranks findings by severity and gives management a crisper statement. A adds useful points about time-on-row and skewed per-category accuracy.
